My working principles.

After Albers · Bauhaus Vorkurs
01 Bauhaus, 1919

Solve the right problem, not the loudest one.

The problem someone hands you is almost never the right problem. It is the version they had time to write down. A good designer spends the first day of any project asking, quietly, what the real problem is. Sometimes it is what they were told. More often, it is one layer deeper. The Bauhaus school in 1919 made every student spend six months on colour and shape before touching a real product. They believed the preparation was the work. They were right.

After Lissitzky · Constructivism, 1922
02 Constructivism, 1917

Most of design is invisible.

You can see a button. You cannot see why the button is where it is. You can see a form. You cannot see why it has five fields instead of two. Most of what a designer decides is invisible: the order things appear in, the defaults, the moment something shows up, the rule that picks which price you see first. The Constructivists knew this. They designed posters, but they also designed the print shop, the delivery truck, the factory floor. The visible thing was only the last step in a long chain of choices.

After Giotto · Scrovegni Chapel, 1305
03 Giotto, c. 1305

A good story is not decoration. It is the argument.

Most designers treat storytelling as wrapping paper on a finished project. Nice fonts, a good headline, a case study PDF. It is a mistake. The story is not around the work. The story is the work. Giotto painted the Scrovegni Chapel in 1305 to teach a Bible story to people who could not read. The pictures were the story. There was no separation. Designers who cannot tell what they are doing and why cannot make anything worth doing.

After Picasso · Analytical Cubism, 1910
04 Cubism, 1907

Design the infrastructure. It is what lasts.

Borrowed from a co-worker.

Most of what I have designed you cannot see. The order that products show up in a search. The default a new user gets. The naming of a status. The moment a notification fires. The rule that decides which price a customer sees first. This is infrastructure. It is where the real decisions live and where most designers never go, because it does not look like design work. It looks like engineering, or product, or operations. It is design work. When it is right, the surface becomes easy to get right. When it is wrong, no amount of surface polish will save it.
